harold-hamm.reviewDepth: Source-led review of the stated episode; not independently editorially reviewed
harold-hamm.period: Second Trump administration, 2025–2026 (reporting dated December 2025 and May 2026)
harold-hamm.summary: Reporting describes a long-running political relationship between Harold Hamm and Donald Trump, large campaign giving, and federal permitting and regulatory actions that benefited Hamm’s company Continental Resources. Outlets and critics link these; the agency denies individual favoritism, and no exchange or wrongdoing has been established.
harold-hamm.mechanism: Campaign giving and personal access to the president and Interior leadership → reported regulatory and permitting benefit; causation unproven

support.text: The Boston Globe reports that Hamm gave more than $2 million to Trump campaigns, helped organize a 2024 Mar-a-Lago oil-executive dinner, and that Energy Secretary Chris Wright is a former director of an industry lobbying group Hamm co-founded. It lists federal actions benefiting Continental, including new Converse County drilling permits, shorter permit reviews and a delayed Biden-era methane fee. Hamm called the Wright and Burgum appointments a “dream team.”
support.source: The Boston Globe: oilman who pushed Trump on fossil fuels
support.access: Page text reviewed via fetch summary; Hamm and Continental declined comment

support.text: High Country News, with Public Domain and Fieldnotes, reports records showing a Continental request to BLM for Converse County permits that avoided an enjoined environmental analysis, pushed by an Interior official, and an April 2025 Hamm meeting with an aide to Secretary Burgum. Continental donated $250,000 to Burgum’s 2024 run. BLM approved 71 new Continental wells. Hamm said regulatory hurdles being removed “does lower our cost of doing business.”
support.source: High Country News / Public Domain: Interior delivered permits for Burgum ally
support.access: Page text reviewed; domain advocacy-oriented outlet, records not independently examined

counter.text: An Interior spokesperson said permitting is “based on agency policy — not on any individual or company,” and the White House described Hamm as one of several executives who advise the president. Hamm and Continental did not respond to the Globe.
counter.source: The Boston Globe: agency and White House responses

counter.text: The reporters say it is unclear what Hamm and Burgum discussed in April 2025, so the article does not establish that the meeting affected permitting. The 2020 environmental analysis was vacated in February 2026 and the ruling is under appeal; Interior’s only reported statement was that Burgum complied with ethics requirements and did not address the emails.
counter.source: High Country News: stated limits of the evidence

harold-hamm.limitations: Scoped to the 2025–2026 oil-and-gas policy and Converse County episode, not Hamm’s whole career. Policies such as permit streamlining and methane-fee changes apply industry-wide; lawful advocacy and donations are not bribery, and no investigation or finding of an improper exchange was found. Both main sources report on, and quote, critics; the WyoFile coverage and company filings were not read. The family entry is scored on Harold Hamm’s personal conduct only.

charles-ergen.reviewDepth: Source-led review of the stated episode; not independently editorially reviewed
charles-ergen.period: FCC inquiry and spectrum sales, May 2025–March 2026
charles-ergen.summary: In 2025 the FCC chair closed an inquiry into EchoStar’s spectrum buildout and confirmed its exclusive rights to a valuable block while EchoStar was selling spectrum to AT&T and SpaceX. A Wall Street Journal editorial reports Ergen met President Trump beforehand. The record shows an unusually favorable regulatory outcome, not a documented payment or bargain.
charles-ergen.mechanism: Personal access to the president → reported regulatory relief enabling large spectrum sales; exchange undocumented

support.text: Reuters reports FCC Chair Carr’s letter to Ergen asking staff to close the investigation, conclude EchoStar met its 5G buildout obligations, and confirm exclusive rights to the AWS-4 spectrum being sold to SpaceX for $17 billion; EchoStar had also agreed to sell spectrum to AT&T for $23 billion. The investigation began in May 2025 after concerns about slow deployment and a SpaceX “warehousing” complaint.
support.source: Reuters via Yahoo Finance: FCC to end EchoStar probe

support.text: A Wall Street Journal editorial, reposted by the Benton Institute, states Ergen met Trump in June 2025 to try to stop the FCC reclaiming EchoStar’s licenses and that Trump “prodded Chairman Carr to let Ergen sell his licenses.” This is opinion-page characterization, not an official record.
support.source: Wall Street Journal editorial board via Benton Institute
support.access: Repost text reviewed; original not read

counter.text: Carr said the deals could be a “potential game changer for the American consumer,” that the status quo “wasn’t working,” and noted Boost Mobile had lost about 2 million subscribers. That is a competition and consumer-benefit rationale for the outcome.
counter.source: Reuters via Yahoo Finance: Carr’s stated rationale

counter.text: The same editorial says the public interest lies in getting scarce spectrum to those who can use it, and notes that the 2019 merger conditions that created Dish as a fourth carrier also came from a Trump administration. It does not allege payments to officials.
counter.source: Wall Street Journal editorial board via Benton Institute: policy framing

charles-ergen.limitations: Scoped to the 2025 EchoStar spectrum episode. No campaign giving, payment or private benefit to officials was found in the pages read, so the feedback dimension is weak. EchoStar’s own statements and the FCC letter itself were not obtained (one trade-press page returned 403). Sale proceeds accrue to the company, in which Ergen is a controlling holder; the personal share was not examined.

johann-rupert.summary: The reviewed pages show Rupert as an outspoken critic of the Zuma-era government and the target of allegations that he influenced a December 2015 finance-minister reversal. Both he and Ramaphosa denied the meeting. No page read documents state patronage or preferential state benefit. The entry concerns Johann Rupert, not other family members.

support.text: Moneyweb reports claims that Deputy President Ramaphosa met senior business people including Rupert after Nene was fired in December 2015, and that this may have influenced Gordhan’s appointment. These are reported claims, not findings.
support.source: Moneyweb via The Citizen: Ramaphosa denies tycoon ties

counter.text: The Presidency said Ramaphosa “categorically denies ever having such a meeting” with Rupert, and Rupert also denied meeting him.

At Richemont’s 2017 AGM Rupert said “radical economic transformation is just a code word for theft”; context includes the state-capture reports and a Bell Pottinger campaign against him. This shows political opposition to the government, not state patronage.
counter.source: Bloomberg via News24: Rupert at Richemont AGM

johann-rupert.limitations: Searched Rupert with Zuma, Ramaphosa, Richemont and Remgro; found 2016–2017 controversy coverage only. Nothing current, and no review of Remgro or Richemont state contracts, tax, or party funding. This is a narrow review and is not exoneration: absence of a documented link in the pages read does not show that none exists. Wealth, nationality, office-holding, honours and company size are not scored, so no estimate is assigned.
